I was raised Roman Catholic to fifth grade and studied with Jehovah’s Witnesses before placing my faith in Jesus at age 22. For the next three years, I was discipled under Pentecostal theologies within the Assemblies of God denomination. I completed my baccalaureate degree in Bible Theology, a Master’s degree in Biblical and Theological Studies, and another in Christian Leadership from evangelical schools resistant to Pentecostalism. My journey and theological assumptions have been continually challenged. I affirm the historic church's rule of faith as expressed in the Creeds but live as one whose allegiance is to the risen Jesus whose kingdom is a present reality in the world. I seek to focus on core theological commitments rather than denominational distinctives.

each Wednesday. Teenagers and I sit around a table, talk about life, and share pizza. Being present among students has significantly changed our interpersonal relationships and conversations. I am no longer inclined to control outcomes or force my agenda on others but am free to enter into life with teens and listen to their stories. The drive to change them has been replaced with a desire to love them. A space has been opened for genuine dialogue. To evaluate one’s theological tradition should never be worrisome. It may present challenges and that is OK. Most importantly, it allows God to kindle within us a fresh imagination of his goodness and grace.

meta.title: Our Theological Traditions Shape Who We Become: How Do We Evaluate Those Traditions?
meta.summary: Examining inherited theology exposes blind spots and helps Christians meet their neighbors with humility, openness, and a reconciling imagination.
